summary:
Czechia's Constitutional Court on 24 April 2024, in judgment PL. US 52/23, struck down the requirement that surgery including sterilisation be a condition for official legal sex change, holding that recognition conditional on disabling reproductive function is unconstitutional, and gave the government until June 2025 to change the law. Reuters reported in June 2025 that the surgery requirement had been dropped, and in July 2025 the Czech Health Ministry announced that trans people would no longer be required to undergo surgery or hormone treatment to change legal gender. Trans*Parent welcomed the change but warned that full legislative reform was still needed to prevent a new government or minister from reversing it. On 12 September 2025 the European Court of Human Rights, in T.H. v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 33037/22), found a violation of Article 8 in the surgical and sterilisation condition and the related civil-registry treatment, with Transgender Europe and ILGA-Europe intervening, and framed Convention-guaranteed recognition through self-determination.

Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1962, homosexual prostitution was decriminalised in 1990, and the age of consent was equalised at 15 in 1990, having previously been 18 for homosexuals. The 2009 Anti-Discrimination Act prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, education, housing and access to goods and services.

Registered partnerships for same-sex couples took effect on 1 July 2006 after a presidential veto was overturned. A 2024 compromise law enshrined same-sex partnerships in the civil code, equating them to marriage in all aspects except joint adoption while permitting step-child adoption, and took effect on 1 January 2025. Individual adoption is permitted and the ban on adoption by those in a registered partnership was struck down in 2016, but joint adoption by same-sex couples remains unavailable. A marriage-equality bill introduced in 2018 by 46 MPs from six parliamentary clubs and backed by the caretaker government cleared parliamentary committees in June 2023, while a constitutional ban on same-sex marriage advanced to second reading with backing from SPD, ODS, KDU-ČSL and ANO. Since 2001, persons living in a common household have held hospital and prison visitation rights similar to those of married heterosexual couples, alongside inheritance and housing succession rights.

Detention practice is inconsistent. In March 2023 the Supreme Administrative Court rebuked the Prague Municipal Court for what it described as sarcastic moral lectures toward an HIV-positive trans man in transition held in immigration detention, and ruled that authorities must first assess whether a detainee is a potentially vulnerable person before deciding placement. In November 2025 the Supreme Court demanded that the national prison concept explicitly address the needs of people in or after transition, with the human-rights commissioner pressing for a binding regulation while the Justice Ministry maintained that the existing framework suffices; that consultation remains open.

Hate-crime protection is in flux. The government approved a Criminal Code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to disability, sexual orientation and gender identity, which remains pending in Parliament, while a Constitutional Court ruling weakened the status of 'particularly vulnerable victim'. The Criminal Code amendments abandon the hostility model for a discriminatory-selection model. The OSCE/ODIHR 2024 hate crime report records 94 hate crimes reported to police in Czechia in 2024, 46 prosecuted and 42 sentenced, with LGBTI-motivated incidents included in the bias breakdown; these are raw counts without a population denominator. ODIHR's key observation is that recorded statistics still do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other crimes.

An ILGA-Europe survey of LGBTQ+ people in Czechia found that 43% had experienced discrimination or harassment in the previous five years, with the highest rates among trans and non-binary respondents, and that 51% had been targeted by insults, assault or threats over five years. Reported anti-LGBT speech by politicians rose from 43% in 2018 to 71% in 2023, and 63% of respondents attributed rising intolerance to politicians. After the Constitutional Court ruling, the Justice Minister publicly stated that his goal was 'to prevent men from giving birth', and other politicians issued transphobic statements; the far-right SPD circulated election leaflets promising to take money from 'LGBT activists'. On 27 June 2021 President Miloš Zeman said that sex-reassignment surgery means 'you are committing a crime for inflicting self-harm' and that 'these transgenders truly disgust me', and said he did not understand transgender people at all.

Public expression is legal and visible but carries social risk. The first Prague Pride parade was held in August 2011 with mayoral support and drew negative responses from religious conservative groups and the far right, and has run annually since 2012. In June 2023 a group disrupted a Brno Pride drag story-time event with homophobic slurs. In April 2023 the Ostrava Regional Court ordered that certificates and diplomas be re-issued to a trans graduate.
tangentialFactors:
Czechia's Asylum Law includes sexual orientation and gender identity grounds and offers an opposite-gender interview option for applicants.

Travel guidance for LGBTQ+ solo travellers rates Prague and Brno highest, citing formal nondiscrimination policies, and locates harassment risk in rural areas and late-night settings.

A 2012 EU Fundamental Rights Agency survey of 93,000 LGBTQ people found that only one in five Czech respondents was open about their orientation to all colleagues or classmates, 71% were selectively open at work or school, and 52% of gay men and 30% of lesbian women avoided holding hands in public outside gay neighbourhoods for fear of assault, threat or harassment. The figures predate the current legal regime.
localsOnly:
Transition-related care is prescribed through Sexology after at least one year of living in the preferred social role with positive psychology and endocrinology evaluations; sexologists may require additional evaluations or withhold treatment for any period. Transgender-related surgeries require approval by a Ministry of Health committee after one year of hormonal treatment, a change of first name to a neutral one, and divorce if the person is married, because the process changes the gender marker.

Military service: a trans woman was refused entry in 2004 and another trans recruit was rejected in 2014 for an alleged reduction in the morale of combat units, but by 2015 trans identity of candidates was no longer considered relevant to service. The Army has allowed homosexuals to serve openly without questioning orientation, and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in the military has been prohibited since 1999.

School curriculum content on LGBTI topics prompted organised parental opt-out campaigns.

Since 1 July 2024 all citizens may donate blood regardless of partner gender, replacing the previous exclusion of people with a same-gender partner; people reporting anal sex with a new partner in the past four months remain excluded.
outOfScopeNotes:
No transgender-specific public-opinion polling is available for Czechia. The acceptance polling cited in the sources concerns homosexuality, same-sex marriage, registered partnerships and gay or lesbian neighbours or acquaintances, and the only transgender-specific attitudinal statement documented is the former president's remarks of 27 June 2021.

The July 2025 change to legal gender recognition was announced by the Health Ministry rather than enacted in statute, and Trans*Parent has warned that a new government or minister could reverse it. Whether the June 2025 deadline set by the Constitutional Court has been met by legislation is unresolved in the sources.

The Criminal Code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to gender identity remains pending in Parliament, so its enactment is not sourced.

The prison regulation sought by the human-rights commissioner remains under consultation, with the Justice Ministry disputing that a new binding rule is needed.

ODIHR notes that recorded hate-crime statistics do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other crimes, so the 2024 figures cannot be read as a complete count of bias-motivated crime.
